summary: A periodic index memo from the RFC Editor summarizing the RFCs numbered 3100 through 3199. It helps readers find and skim documents published in that range. It is a catalog, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a librarian making a list of the hundred newest books on the shelf, with one line about each. This memo is that list for a batch of Internet documents.

subtitle: A directory of the hundred RFCs published in 2001-2003.

tldr.problem: As the RFC series grew to thousands of documents, readers needed a way to find and understand what was published in a given period.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Editor periodically publishes an index memo listing each RFC in a hundred-number range with a short summary of its purpose.
tldr.outcome: Readers can use these summary memos to browse, search, or locate RFCs from a specific era without reading full documents.

today: RFC 3199 is informational and remains published. It serves as a historical record and reference guide for the 99 RFCs it summarizes. The individual RFCs it lists have their own current statuses, which should be verified in the latest RFC index.

sections.title: What This Memo Is
sections.content:
RFC 3199 is an annotated list of the 100 RFCs published from number 3100 through 3199. It is a catalog issued by the RFC Editor in February 2003, shortly after the last RFC in the range was published.

Each entry names the RFC number, its author, publication date, and title, followed by a one or two sentence summary of the document's purpose. Some RFCs are marked as on the standards track; others are informational or experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC editor counted 100 RFCs that had just come out and wrote down what each one was about in one or two sentences.

sections.title: Why We Need These Memos
sections.content:
By 2003, the RFC series had published three thousand documents on widely different topics: protocols, best practices, terminology guides, jokes, and historical records. Without indexes, readers had to search blindly or ask colleagues for pointers.

The RFC Editor publishes these summary memos regularly, usually after every hundred RFCs are issued. They serve two purposes: they provide a snapshot of what was published in a era, and they are less daunting than the full RFC texts for someone browsing for something new.
sections.plainLanguage: When there are thousands of documents, you need a list of what the newest ones are about so you can find the ones you want to read.

sections.title: What Was Published in RFC 3100-3199
sections.content:
The batch covers the period from May 2001 to January 2003. It includes protocols for routing (OSPF enhancements, RSIP, BGP label mapping), security (S/MIME, IPsec, X.509 certificates), network management (SNMP MIB extensions, policy frameworks), and media types (RTP payloads for audio and video, XHTML registration).

It also includes terminology documents (AAA evaluation, FIB benchmarking), operational guidance (IPv6 address allocation, DNSSEC status), and standards-track improvements to TCP congestion control and DNS security. RFC 3100 was never issued; the count begins with 3101.
sections.plainLanguage: This batch has new rules for routing, ways to send data securely, tools to manage networks, and ways to mark different kinds of files.

sections.title: The Standards Track Note
sections.content: The memo includes a note that many RFCs in the batch are on the IETF standards track. The standards track has three levels: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and Standard. Since the status of documents can change as the IETF processes them, the memo does not assert a fixed status. Readers who need to know the current status of an RFC should consult the latest "Internet Official Protocol Standards" document, also published by the RFC Editor.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these documents are on a path to becoming official Internet rules, but the rules can change, so check the latest official list before relying on them.

sections.title: Using This Index Today
sections.content: This memo is itself informational and historical. It remains useful as a reference for what was published during a specific period and as a quick-start guide to the hundred RFCs it summarizes. However, it has not aged well for assessing the current status of any individual RFC. For that, consult the RFC index itself or the current standards document.
sections.plainLanguage: This list is still useful for seeing what was published in 2001-2003, but to know if any of those documents are still official rules, you need to check a newer list.
